status: DRAFT. Every item needs clinician approval before release. Items with evidence L are optional.

evidence_labels.R: Randomised trial or systematic review / meta-analysis

caveats.exercise: Always add: if your doctor says it is fine. Safety outcomes were not reported in the trials.
caveats.sleep_hygiene: Recommended for sleep problems in pregnancy. Do not claim it prevents or treats depression.
caveats.mindfulness_breathing: Controlled trials show limited benefit. Optional.

suggestions.text: This was a balanced week. That's worth noticing and being proud of.
Keep your sleep and meals steady, and rest whenever you can.
Gentle regular movement, like walking or yoga a few times a week, can help your mood. Check with your doctor that it is right for you.
Stay connected with people who support you, and keep talking openly with them.
Pick one enjoyable or meaningful thing to look forward to next week.
Now is a good time to plan who can help with night time, meals and childcare after the baby arrives.
Keep accepting help from family and friends. It makes a real difference.
A week with ups and downs is completely normal, especially at this time of life.
Try to do one small enjoyable or meaningful thing each day, even for ten minutes.
A walk or gentle yoga a few times a week can lift your mood, if your doctor says it is fine.
A steady bedtime routine, less caffeine and quieter evenings can help you sleep.
Is there one task someone could help with this week?
Take a few minutes just for yourself each day.
Ask someone to cover one night feed so you can get a longer stretch of sleep.
Start small. Choose one simple activity you can manage today, like a short walk, a call or a warm meal.
If something is worrying you, break it into small steps and try just one.
Is there one person you could talk to today? Share how you feel with a partner, family member or friend, and accept help when it is offered.
A support group for mothers can help. Talking with someone who understands often feels good.
Gentle movement such as walking or yoga can help, if your doctor says it is fine.
Prioritise rest where you can, and keep to a regular bedtime and wake-up time.
Eat regular meals and drink enough water, even on hard days.
Deep breathing, gentle stretching or a few minutes of quiet can help you feel calmer.
On the hardest days, aim for one or two things, like eating something and resting. That is enough.
Talking to your doctor or health worker can open up options such as guided self-help or talking support. Would you like help preparing for that?
Mention how you have been feeling at your next antenatal visit. Counselling during pregnancy can help.
Keep your early postnatal check-ups and tell your health worker how you have been feeling.
Keep regular times for sleeping, waking and eating. A steady daily rhythm helps protect your mood.
suggestions.note: S7 evidence is from bipolar disorder, not specifically perinatal.

suggestions.text: Wind down before bed and keep caffeine to the morning.
Is there someone close to you who could notice how you're doing this week? It helps to have a person who can spot early changes.
If you are sleeping much less than usual but still feel full of energy, please tell your doctor or midwife soon.
Plan for night time support so you can have a longer stretch of sleep.
Try to keep this week's commitments to the essentials.
Feeling anxious is common during and after pregnancy. It is worth mentioning to your doctor or health worker.
A guided, CBT-based self-help programme over a couple of months is one option your health worker can arrange.
Slow breathing, gentle yoga or quiet time can help you feel calmer.
Feeling short-tempered when tired is common. Resting and sharing tasks can help.
Your sleep has been steady, a real support for your mood.
A consistent bedtime routine, avoiding caffeine and slowing down before bed can help.
If you are not asleep after about 15 minutes, get up and move to another room until you feel sleepy. Short daytime naps can also help.
Broken sleep is expected with a newborn. Plan night time support if you can, and rest whenever possible.
If poor sleep keeps going, tell your doctor. Talking-based sleep programmes (CBT for insomnia) are the standard first treatment for insomnia.
suggestions.note: Not yet shown to prevent depression. Do not claim that.

suggestions.text: You've been sleeping a lot and feeling low. It might be worth mentioning to your doctor.

tougher: This week had some heavier days. Many mothers go through patches like this, and you don't have to handle it alone.
Thank you for checking in even when it was hard.
high_energy: You've had a lot of energy this week, which can feel great. Let's make sure rest keeps up.
good: This was a balanced week. That's worth noticing and being proud of.
okay: A week with ups and downs is completely normal, especially at this time of life.
